title: Liquid Hydrogen Storage Tank Design
short_description: A team research report on hydrogen as a transport fuel, culminating in an original tank design that captures boil-off hydrogen in a metal-organic framework instead of venting it.
full_description: A team research report — "Hydrogen: The Fuel of the Future?" — investigating the barriers to a hydrogen economy (cost, public perception, production, storage) and proposing an original dual-chamber storage tank that adsorbs boil-off hydrogen into a metal-organic framework (MOF) instead of venting it to the atmosphere.
motivation: Transport accounts for around 24% of direct CO2 emissions from fuel combustion, and hydrogen's high gravimetric energy makes it an appealing zero-emission alternative. The team also investigated the public-perception barrier left by the 1937 Hindenburg disaster — a survey of 182 people I designed and ran found only 35.2% believed hydrogen was a safe transport fuel — and chose to focus the invention on the technical problem, storage losses, that most directly limits hydrogen's practicality.
methodology: After researching hydrogen production methods (electrolysis, natural gas reforming, thermochemical water splitting) and storage options (compressed gas, liquid hydrogen, metal hydrides, MOFs), the team designed a dual-chamber tank: liquid hydrogen sits in a vacuum-insulated left chamber, and instead of venting the gas that boils off as it warms, a pressure valve routes it into a second chamber packed with MOF-74 (using a Ni2+ cation for the highest adsorption rate), which adsorbs the evaporated hydrogen instead of releasing it. Tank dimensions were derived from a fixed 1:8 radius-to-length ratio at a 5000L capacity, and I produced the 3D model renders of the tank design.
results: For a 5000L tank losing 15% of its liquid hydrogen to boil-off per 24 hours, the design was calculated to need 16.73kg of MOF-74 to adsorb all the evaporated gas — saving a net ~7,300MJ of energy per day that would otherwise be lost through venting.
lessons_learned: Follow-on improvements identified: running the MOF compartment at higher pressure to improve adsorption and reduce waste further, and pairing the vacuum layer with foam insulation for better thermal performance without adding significant weight or cost.
